ch07 - Introduction.md
chapters.relation: Frames the volume with Morpheus's red-pill speech in The Matrix, treating the rabbit-hole as our culture's portal of escape and asking how to make sense of what we find in Wonderland: hookah-smoking caterpillars, babies that turn into pigs, grins without cats, and trials where the sentence comes before the evidence. It takes Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the book's guiding question, tying knowledge of who we are and can become to memory of who we have been, and previews chapters on the feminist Alice, the Red Queen and nuclear strategy, mushroom trips, and the connection between Alice, procrastination, and the Spice Girls.

chapters.file: ch08 - PART ONE - “WAKE UP, ALICE DEAR”.md
ch09 - NOTES.md
chapters.relation: Argues that Alice, in Carroll's and Disney's versions, is a feminist model who navigates Wonderland by her own wits, unlike passive princesses such as Cinderella and Aurora who need male rescue. Megan S. Lloyd reads Alice's fall down the rabbit-hole as a rejection of her sister's idle female role, the Pigeon's complaints and the Duchess's shaken pig-baby as showing that motherhood is not a requirement of female worth, and the Mad Hatter's 'Then you shouldn't talk' as the old-boy network punishing an assertive woman. Alice's final 'You're nothing but a pack of cards!' completes her growth into a powerful presence, and the chapter closes by asking what twenty-first-century young women facing double standards would do if they asked 'What would Alice do?'

chapters.file: ch10 - “Some People Have No More Sense Than a Baby!”.md
chapters.relation: Uses the White Queen's 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' to introduce Elijah Millgram's jam-yesterday-jam-tomorrow goods: jobs, parenting, and Utah hiking that feel drudging in every moment yet are remembered and anticipated as wonderful. Mark D. White brings in G. E. Moore's organic unity, illustrated by the Spice Girls' 'Wannabe', Wham!, and Led Zeppelin, to ask how a whole made entirely of bad parts can be good 'on the whole', then treats procrastination as akrasia (weakness of will) and endorses Millgram's remedy: manufacture short-term 'jam today' goals like graduation ceremonies and marked lookout points to motivate timely action.

chapters.file: ch11 - Grand Masters of the Universe.md
chapters.relation: Chases Cold War nuclear strategists down the rabbit-hole, reading the Mad Tea Party as the MAD (mutually assured destruction) tea party where 'to reduce the risk of nuclear war, the risk must be increased' passes for wisdom. Ron Hirschbein uses Wittgenstein's language games (Alice was his favorite English prose), Rorty's final vocabulary, and Derrida's remark that a nuclear war has never 'taken place' to argue that Nukespeak, deterrence, the 'Delicate Balance of Terror', and the post hoc ergo propter hoc argument for deterrence are ungrounded, unfalsifiable word games. The Queen of Hearts's 'Off with his head!' prefigures decapitation strategy and the Hitler card, and the looking-glass chessboard becomes the arms race in which the public are expendable pawns.

chapters.file: ch12 - A Closer Look at Alice’s Trial.md
chapters.relation: Argues Alice is right to attack the court of the King and Queen of Hearts because she never entered a social contract with Wonderland: unlike Socrates, who stayed in Athens and so had to abide by the verdict (Plato's Crito), Alice fell in involuntarily and is trying to leave. Dennis Knepp casts the Queen of Hearts as Hobbes's absolute sovereign whose public 'Off with their heads!' terrorizes the playing cards into obedience ('Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words'), while Locke's limited, consent-based government and Rawls's contractualism mark the better alternative the Hearts court fails to meet. Since Alice stands outside their covenant, she is her own more-than-a-mile-high Leviathan, rightly defending herself in the state of nature.

chapters.file: ch13 - PART TWO - “THAT’S LOGIC”.md
ch14 - “Consider Your Verdict!”.md
chapters.relation: Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Lasting Legacy of Logic.md
chapters.relation: Treats Carroll the Oxford logician as a teacher hiding five lessons in Wonderland: watch your assumptions (the King infers the Knave's guilt from an unsigned letter), know what your words mean (Humpty Dumpty on 'glory'), don't confuse categories (the King's 'Nobody' and the Hatter's personified Time), don't switch subjects and predicates ('I mean what I say' versus 'I say what I mean'), and don't confuse necessary with sufficient conditions (Alice's Ada and Mabel arguments, with a hammer-and-egg illustration). David S. Brown grounds the lessons in Hume on causes discoverable only by experience, Aristotle's law of non-contradiction and categories, the Marx Brothers' 'Either he's dead or my watch has stopped', and Popper's point that a successful prediction cannot prove a hypothesis, only a failed one can refute it.

chapters.file: ch16 - Wonderland and the Real World.md
chapters.relation: Extracts three problems of induction from Alice's misadventures: predicting the future (Hume's problem: nothing rationally compels Humpty Dumpty to agree the world will not turn into Wonderland at 6 a.m. tomorrow), proving whose dream it is (Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence: Tweedledee can accommodate any evidence within the theory that Alice exists only in the Red King's dream), and translating Wonderese (Quine's indeterminacy: pointing at the White Rabbit cannot fix whether natives mean the rabbit, its parts, or its stages, nor what 'muchness' means). Brendan Shea shows Alice succeeding where the creatures fail by the criteria Hume and Quine endorse: experimentation, simplicity, conservatism of belief, and a principle of charity in translation.

chapters.file: ch17 - “Language Is Worth a Thousand Pounds a Word”.md
chapters.relation: Pits Donald Davidson's notorious claim that 'there is no such thing as a language' against the Wonderland dialogues, asking whether communication rests on shared rules (the institutional view) or on speaker intentions (the invention view). Daniel Whiting argues that 'curiouser and curiouser', the Mock Turtle's 'uglification', and the Mouse's tale/tail homophony show grasp of rules is neither necessary nor sufficient for understanding, as Davidson holds, but that Humpty Dumpty's 'which is to be master—that's all', the Red Queen's 'when you've once said a thing, that fixes it', and Alice's talks with the Sheep and the March Hare show the invention view is solipsistic too, so rule-governed established meanings still do real work in conversation.

chapters.file: ch18 - PART THREE - “WE’RE ALL MAD HERE”.md
ch19 - Perceptions Are Fine, but Dull Reality Is Still Better.md
chapters.relation: Distinguishes perceiver, perceptions, and perceived external objects to ask whether Alice, or anyone, can get beyond her perceptions to a mind-independent world, entering through Robert Arp's own painkiller hallucination of stones that were really Jell-O. The chapter sets epistemological idealism and metaphysical antirealism (the movie-theater-in-the-mind picture, traced to Plato's cave and Berkeley's suggestion that we are trapped inside perceptual reality) against the epistemological and metaphysical realism it finds in Alice and Carroll: fossilized ferns, dodo birds, and the Pythagorean theorem are discovered rather than invented, and at story's end everything rightly changes 'to dull reality'.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Real Is Fake and the Fake Is Real.md
chapters.relation: Takes Morpheus's red-pill speech at face value to ask whether Alice is a drug story, then argues the deeper point: the distinction between normal and distorted experience is exaggerated or specious because all perception is conditioned by expectation, mood, and chemistry, whether on caffeine or psilocybin. Scott F. Parker reads the Red King's dream alongside Plato's Theaetetus dream argument and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream to show we can never prove we are awake, then weighs William James's nitrous-oxide revelations and Aldous Huxley's mescaline 'Mind at Large' as reasons altered states might sometimes show reality more truly, concluding that the real is fake, the fake is real, and Wonderland's syndrome is now a recognized medical condition.

chapters.file: ch21 - Dull Reality The Tragic View of Life.md
chapters.relation: A Nietzschean interpretation: Alice's unastonished pursuit of the White Rabbit exemplifies the 'will to ignorance' hidden within the will to truth, since every perspective is created by selecting and simplifying while we convince ourselves we have discovered rather than invented. Rick Mayock reads the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and the mushroom as lessons in perspectivism and in the self as a grammatical fiction (no doer behind the deed, no lightning behind the flash), the Queen's beheadings and ruleless croquet as a flux of competing wills to power, and the Hatter's madness as Dionysian against Alice's Apollonian calm, with Greek tragedy supplying the metaphysical comfort that makes 'dull reality' livable.

chapters.file: ch22 - Deleuze Jam Today.md
chapters.relation: Walks Alice through four theories of time: Augustine's three presents in Confessions (Alice 'was a different person then'; the past exists only as present memory), Kant's time as a subjective form of intuition presupposed by experience (the White Rabbit's anxiety about being late already requires it), Bergson's indivisible duration against spatialized clock time (running fastest with the Red Queen yet ending under the same tree; the Hatter stuck at six o'clock; Zeno's Achilles resolved by indivisible acts), and Deleuze's chronos and aion from The Logic of Sense. Mark W. Westmoreland reads 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' as pure aion: the present never arrives, only an endlessly subdividing past-future.

chapters.file: ch23 - PART FOUR - “WHO IN THE WORLD AM I ”.md
ch24 - A Nonsense Too Far.md
chapters.relation: Places Carroll's nonsense in a Greco-Roman tradition of philosophically useful absurdity: Socrates exposing Euthyphro's definitions of piety as nonsense, Plato's tongue-in-cheek Republic calculation that the tyrant's life is 729 times worse, and Diogenes ridiculing slavery even while sold on the auction block. Charles Taliaferro and Elizabeth Olson argue the jokes land only because Alice stays sane, curious, polite, and self-controlled, the stable foil who keeps the death threats and cruelty of Wonderland and the Looking-Glass on the amusing side of the ledger, and that nonsense goes 'too far' in Kafka's The Trial, where losing the sane, good center turns absurdity into meaninglessness.

chapters.file: ch25 - From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory.md
chapters.relation: Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.

holes.name: Organic Unity (Moore)
holes.what: Moore's Principia Ethica doctrine that the value of a whole need not equal the sum of the values of its parts.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses organic unity to explain how experiences bad in every moment (jam-yesterday-jam-tomorrow goods like jobs and parenting) can still be good 'on the whole', illustrated by bands like the Spice Girls.

holes.name: Donald Davidson
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of language and mind who denied that a language is a shared system of conventions and grounded communication in the charitable interpretation of speaker intentions.
holes.why: Chapter 17 is built entirely on Davidson's 'there is no such thing as a language' thesis, tested against Humpty Dumpty, 'uglification', and Wonderland malapropisms.

holes.name: Passing Theories (convention-free communication)
holes.what: Davidson's view that hearers improvise a 'passing theory' of each utterance's intended meaning, so shared rules are neither necessary nor sufficient for communication.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses it to explain how Alice understands 'curiouser and curiouser' and 'uglification' despite rule-breaking, while arguing the invention view cannot dispense with established meanings.

holes.name: Chronos and Aion (Deleuze's two readings of time)
holes.what: Deleuze's distinction in The Logic of Sense between Chronos, where only the present fills time, and Aion, where only an infinitely subdivided past-future exists and the present never arrives.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads the White Queen's 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' as aion: today never comes, it is always yesterday and tomorrow together.
